system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2172-02-05 19:53:00 to 2172-02-06 17:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for a non-healing abdominal wound following a prior open gastrostomy tube placement. She underwent reopening and debridement of the wound with removal of a retained suture acting as a foreign body. Postoperatively, she remained stable, afebrile, and in good condition with well-controlled pain. Oral antibiotics were started to prevent infection, and her home medications, including those for glycemic control, were resumed. She tolerated the procedure well and was discharged the following morning with instructions for wound care, antibiotic use, and follow-up with surgery clinic. No complications arose during the brief admission.
problems: Other specified complications of procedures not elsewhere classified
Surgical operation with formation of external stoma causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation

Ms. ___ presented on ___ with abdominal pain and 
increasing g-tube discharge since tripping on it three days 
prior.  She was admitted for observation and radiographic 
imaging to rule out a gastric leak.  She had no peritoneal

rash-appearing erythema.

continued to have abdominal pain at the site of granulation 
tissue of the g-tube.  She had persistent g-tube site discharge 
well managed with dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team doctors. You’re here because you had sudden abdominal pain after stepping on your feeding tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I tripped on the tube three days ago, felt a sharp tug, and the pain hasn’t gone away. The area around the tube is also more red and has this yellow discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And are you having nausea, vomiting, or any fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or vomiting. Feeds are going in okay, but the skin around the tube is really irritated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’re going to keep you NPO for now—no tube feeds—just to be safe. We’ll start IV fluids and get some imaging to make sure the tube hasn’t moved or caused a leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they do that tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the radiology team is already setting up a G-tube study. They’ll inject a little contrast to see where it goes and check if there’s any leakage outside the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the scan is back. The tube is in the right place, and the contrast went straight into your stomach and then into the small bowel. No signs of a leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So nothing tore or came loose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the internal part looks intact. But we did see some irritation and granulation tissue at the skin site, which is likely why it’s painful and draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the same thing that happened before, when they found a suture stuck in the wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar, but this time it’s not a foreign body. It’s just the body’s way of healing—sometimes too much tissue forms. We’ll manage it with better wound care and frequent dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are normal—no infection signs. We’re going to restart your tube feeds slowly and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain? It’s better, but still there when I touch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving you pain meds as needed. The discomfort should improve as the skin irritation resolves. The redness has already gotten much better with proper care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating the feeds well, no nausea, and your pain is controlled. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Should I do anything different at home with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing frequent dressing changes, and watch for increased redness, swelling, or foul-smelling discharge. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ in two weeks—he may consider repositioning the tube if the granulation tissue persists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and I can keep taking my regular medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home meds are continued, including the mupirocin for MRSA and your vitamins. We’re adding a stool softener to help with bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was really worried something serious happened.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But you’re stable, healing, and safe to go home. Just call if you develop fever, severe pain, or trouble with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are ready. You’ll get written instructions and prescriptions before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll make sure to keep the site clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep up with the follow-up. We want to make sure this doesn’t keep happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in one last time. Still doing well? No new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, still feeling okay. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted after experiencing persistent abdominal pain and increased discharge from her G-tube following an incident where she stepped on the tube. Initial evaluation raised concern for possible dislodgement or perforation, so she was kept NPO and underwent a G-tube sinogram, which confirmed the tube was correctly positioned with no evidence of leakage. She was restarted on tube feeds, which she tolerated well, and her skin erythema improved with proper wound care. Pain was managed with medication, and she remained stable throughout the admission. She was discharged home with instructions for ongoing wound care, medication management, and follow-up with surgery clinic for possible tube repositioning.
